newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mobutu gives olive branch to rebels as talks start.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu gives olive branch to rebels as talks start.

text.p: Zaire peace negotiations got under way in earnest on Sunday at a secret location somewhere in South Africa, after "organisational" delays.

In an apparent bid for conciliation, Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko told a South African Sunday newspaper that rebel leader Laurent Kabila was a "nationalist patriot" and urged him to make peace for the good of the country.
But analysts said it was difficult to see how the two sides could achieve a compromise that would permit a ceasefire in the six-month-old civil war.
Rebel forces, insisting Mobutu must go, appear to have the run of the country, marching into one town after another meeting no resistance but, instead, only cheers from the people.
They now control over a third of Zaire and have vowed to go all the way to Kinshasa if necessary to force Mobutu out.
"The talks have started," a South African foreign ministry spokesman said.
Representatives of Kabila and negotiators from the Kinshasa government sat down to open substantive discussions at about 0830 GMT, he added.

A South Africa-based representative of the rebel alliance said the delay between Saturday's formal opening of the peace conference, at a high-profile ceremony in Pretoria, and the start of actual talks in secret was due purely to "organisational matters".

The negotiations, brokered by the United Nations and South Africa, got off to a frosty start in Pretoria on Saturday, with rebel envoy Bizima Karaha in effect telling the government delegation it was now or never if they wanted a peaceful settlement.
There has been no indication that Mobutu, who has held on to absolute power for 32 years, is getting ready to quit, although he is suffering from prostate cancer and his government is in disarray.

In an interview published by the South African Sunday Times and conducted at his presidential residence in Kinshasa a few days ago, Mobutu urged rebel leader Laurent Kabila to come to the negotiating table and make peace.

"Kabila is a nationalist patriot. I urge him to come to the table with his Zairian brothers and sisters to restore peace in the country and to contribute to the achievement of the current democratic process," Mobutu told the newspaper.

Mobutu is reputed to have amassed a vast personal fortune while his country sank into economic chaos, rampant poverty and now political disarray. Previous olive-branch offers and power-sharing arrangements proferred by Kinshasa to the rebels have been dismissed out of hand.

"My objective has three points," Mobutu was quoted as saying in written replies to questions put by the newspaper. "To safeguard unity and peace between all sons and daughters of Zaire, to preserve territorial integrity, and to make Zaire a modern democracy."
Asked if he agreed with the perception that Zaire needed change, Mobutu replied that it already had change in the person of himself.
"I am the person who opened up the way to what some call political adjustments or the democratisation process. I believe the democratisation process should not be infringed," he said.
